At its core, Singer argues that we should act in ways that maximize total happiness or well-being across all sentient beings — not just humans, but any creature capable of suffering or pleasure. His famous argument in 'Animal Liberation' extends this principle to animals: if a pig can suffer, its suffering matters morally on equal footing with a human's. He pushes this further with his drowning child thought experiment — the idea that if we're morally obligated to save a drowning child at only moderate inconvenience, we have a similar obligation to give significant portions of our income to global poverty relief, since the cost to us is similarly small while the benefit to a starving person is enormous. The teaching point here is that utilitarianism demands a more impartial view than most people find comfortable: our moral duties extend beyond our immediate circle, and self-interest should not be the primary moral motivator.
